title: Lightning Hit This Park Ranger 7 Times. He Survived Them All #shorts
description:
Case 011. Roy Sullivan was a park ranger in Shenandoah National Park, Virginia. Between 1942 and 1977 he was struck by lightning seven times and survived every strike, which Guinness World Records lists as the most lightning strikes survived by one person. 1942: sheltering in a fire lookout tower, he ran from it and lost a big toenail. 1969: in his truck on a mountain road, he lost his eyebrows. 1970: in his own front yard, his left shoulder was seared. 1972: inside a ranger station, his hair was set on fire. 1973: on patrol, his hair burned again and his legs were seared; he put it out with the can of water he kept in his truck. 1976: an injured ankle. 1977: while he was fishing, burns to his chest and stomach. Two of his ranger hats, with lightning-damaged crowns, went on display in Guinness exhibit halls. He died in 1983, aged 71. Rook didn't believe it either.

Animated reconstruction of a true story. The tower, road, house, station, pond and hall in the film are generic sets, and the cards and lists are drawings made for it, not real documents. Do not shelter under trees or in open structures in a thunderstorm: get indoors or into a closed vehicle.
title_options: Lightning Hit This Park Ranger 7 Times. He Survived Them All #shorts
The Ranger Lightning Could Not Kill #shorts
His Hair Caught Fire Twice. Lightning Still Wasn't Done #shorts
source_notes: Read for this run (fetched 14 Nov 2026): the Guinness World Records page 'Most lightning strikes survived'; Wikipedia (Roy Sullivan); National Parks Traveler (Bob Janiskee, July 2008); The Weather Network ('This Day in Weather History: June 25, 1977', 2021, updated 2023). The spine of the film is the Guinness entry, which gives all seven strikes with what each one did: 1942 (lost big toe nail), 1969 (lost eyebrows), July 1970 (left shoulder seared), 16 April 1972 (hair set on fire), 7 August 1973 (new hair re-fired and legs seared), 5 June 1976 (ankle injured), 25 June 1977 (chest and stomach burns). Every injury named in the narration is one of these. Agreed by the other sources that mention each point: he was a ranger in Shenandoah National Park, Virginia (Wikipedia, National Parks Traveler, Weather Network); strike 1 was at a fire lookout tower in a thunderstorm and he was outside it, moving away, when he was hit (Wikipedia: he 'was said to then have run out' and was struck 'a few feet away'; National Parks Traveler: he said he had 'bailed out of the tower'), which is why the script says he 'runs from a fire tower'; strike 2 was in his truck on a mountain road (Wikipedia, National Parks Traveler), the bolt coming off nearby trees through the open window (Wikipedia only; shown, not narrated); strike 3 was in his front yard (both), off a power transformer (Wikipedia only; shown, not narrated); strike 4 was inside a ranger station (both); for strike 5 he was on patrol, out of or beside his truck (Wikipedia: he had decided 'it was safe to leave his truck'; National Parks Traveler: 'standing near his vehicle'), and he put the fire out with water he kept in the truck (Wikipedia: 'the can of water, which he always kept there'; National Parks Traveler: a container of water in his vehicle that 'he apparently used' in 1973); strike 7 came while he was fishing (Wikipedia, National Parks Traveler, Weather Network); two of his ranger hats are on display in Guinness exhibit halls (Wikipedia; National Parks Traveler adds 'both with lightning-damaged crowns', which is the basis for 'scorched'). Where the sources differ: (1) The sixth strike is 5 June 1976 in Guinness, Wikipedia and The Weather Network but '1974' in National Parks Traveler's tally; the film follows the three. (2) Where the sixth strike happened: Guinness and Wikipedia do not say, National Parks Traveler says a campground; the film shows him on a trail and the narration names no place. (3) 1942: The Weather Network says the tower caught fire, Wikipedia says the new tower had no lightning rod and was hit seven or eight times; the film shows the tower struck and sparks in the cab, no blaze, and the narration says only that he runs from it. Wikipedia and The Weather Network also describe a burn down his right leg and a hole in his shoe; the narration keeps to Guinness's toenail and the drawing shows a scorched boot. (4) 1969: Wikipedia adds that he was knocked unconscious and his hair caught fire; Guinness and National Parks Traveler list the eyebrows; the film shows him dazed and smoking with his eyebrows gone and no flames. (5) 1972: the story that he could not get his head under the tap and used a wet towel is in Wikipedia; National Parks Traveler repeats a version of it (wet paper towels) and says it cannot confirm it. It is shown for under a second and not narrated. (6) 1973: some accounts say he was 'blasted out of his car'; National Parks Traveler says that is wrong, and the film shows him standing by the truck. The often-repeated line that a cloud 'followed' him is his own reported remark (Wikipedia attaches it to 1973 and to 1976) and is not used. (7) When he began as a ranger: 1936 (Wikipedia) or 1940 (National Parks Traveler); not stated in the film. (8) Verification: Wikipedia says the strikes were documented by the park superintendent, R. Taylor Hoskins, and also notes he was not present at any of them; the script therefore says 'Guinness lists them all' and 'Nobody on record has survived more', which is what the Guinness record states, and does not claim independent proof of each strike. Left out on purpose: his death. Guinness, Wikipedia and National Parks Traveler all report that he took his own life in September 1983, six years after the last strike; a 47-second comic-toned Short is not the place for it, so the film ends in 1977 and the description gives only the year and his age. Also left out: the unverified childhood strike he never claimed, his wife being struck while hanging washing, the bear-and-trout story from the day of the seventh strike (Wikipedia only), the nicknames, and any odds figure (National Parks Traveler itself calls the usual calculation bogus because the strikes are not independent events). Paraphrase, not quotation: no words are attributed to anyone. Dramatised, not reported: what the tower, road, truck, gate, house, station, pond, jetty and hall looked like (all generic; the truck has no markings and no badge or agency emblem appears anywhere); what he was doing at the station desk; that the 1977 strike found him on a jetty at dusk (the sources say only 'fishing', Wikipedia 'a freshwater pool'); his hat flying off in strikes 5 and 7; the weather and time of day of every strike; his greying hair (he was 30 in 1942 and 65 in 1977, so the film greys him from 1969); the tally on the chalkboard; the list card (labelled in the film as drawn for it, and as following Guinness's list); and everything Rook does, including the lure he pockets. Rook's jokes are limited to his own reactions (the empty water can, pulling his hat down); for the seventh strike, where the man is burned and was taken to hospital (National Parks Traveler), he kneels with his hat off and says nothing funny.
